4 // Rustan Leino, June 2012.
5 // This file verifies an algorithm, due to Boyer and Moore, that finds the majority choice
6 // among a sequence of votes, see http://www.cs.utexas.edu/~moore/best-ideas/mjrty/.
7 // Actually, this algorithm is a slight variation on theirs, but the general idea for why
8 // it is correct is the same.  In the Boyer and Moore algorithm, the loop counter is advanced
9 // by exactly 1 each iteration, which means that there may or may not be a "current leader".
10 // In my program below, I had instead written the loop invariant to say there is always a
11 // "current leader", which requires the loop index sometimes to skip a value.
12 //
13 // This file has two versions of the algorithm.  In the first version, the given sequence
14 // of votes is assumed to have a (strict) majority choice, meaning that strictly more than
15 // 50% of the votes are for one candidate.  It is convenient to have a name for the majority
16 // choice, in order to talk about it in specifications.  The easiest way to do this in
17 // Dafny is probably to introduce a ghost parameter with the given properties.  That's what
18 // the algorithm does, see parameter K.  The postcondition is thus to output the value of
19 // K, which is done in the non-ghost out-parameter k.
20 // The proof of the algorithm requires two lemmas.  These lemmas are proved automatically
21 // by Dafny's induction tactic.
22 //
23 // In the second version of the program, the main method does not assume there is a majority
24 // choice.  Rather, it eseentially uses the first algorithm and then checks if what it
25 // returns really is a majority choice.  To do this, the specification of the first algorithm
26 // needs to be changed slightly to accommodate the possibility that there is no majority
27 // choice.  That change in specification is also reflected in the loop invariant.  Moreover,
28 // the algorithm itself now needs to extra 'if' statements to see if the entire sequence
29 // has been searched through.  (This extra 'if' is essentially already handled by Boyer and
30 // Moore's algorithm, because it increments the loop index by 1 each iteration and therefore
31 // already has a special case for the case of running out of sequence elements without a
32 // current leader.)
33 // The calling harness, DetermineElection, somewhat existentially comes up with the majority
34 // choice, if there is such a choice, and then passes in that choice as the ghost parameter K
35 // to the main algorithm.  Neat, huh?
36 
37 // Language comment:
38 // The "(==)" that sits after some type parameters in this program says that the actual
39 // type argument must support equality.

40 // Advanced remark:
41 // There is a subtle situation in the verification of DetermineElection.  Suppose the type
42 // parameter Candidate denotes some type whose instances depend on which object are
43 // allocated.  For example, if Candidate is some class type, then more candidates can come
44 // into being by object allocations (using "new").  What does the quantification of
45 // candidates "c" in the postcondition of DetermineElection now mean--all candidates that
46 // existed in the pre-state or (the possibly larger set of) all candidates that exist in the
47 // post-state?  (It means the latter.)  And if there does not exist a candidate in majority
48 // in the pre-state, could there be a (newly created) candidate in majority in the post-state?
49 // This will require some proof.  The simplest argument seems to be that even if more candidates
50 // are created during the course of DetermineElection, such candidates cannot possibly
51 // be in majority in the sequence "a", since "a" can only contain candidates that were already
52 // created in the pre-state.  This property is easily specified by adding a postcondition
53 // to the Count function.  Alternatively, one could have added the antecedent "c in a" or
54 // "old(allocated(c))" to the "forall c" quantification in the postcondition of DetermineElection.

55 // About reading the proofs:
56 // Dafny proves the FindWinner algorithm from the given loop invariants and the two lemmas
57 // Lemma_Unique and Lemma_Split.  In showing this proof to some colleagues, they found they
58 // were not as quick as Dafny in constructing the proof from these ingredients.  For a human
59 // to understand the situation better, it helps to take smaller (and more) steps in the proof.
60 // At the end of this file, Nadia Polikarpova has written two versions of FindWinner that does
61 // that, using Dafny's support for calculational proofs.

80 method FindWinner<Candidate(==)>(a: seq<Candidate>, ghost K: Candidate) returns (k: Candidate)
81   requires HasMajority(a, 0, |a|, K) // K has a (strict) majority of the votes
82   ensures k == K  // find K
83 {
84   k := a[0];
85   var n, c, s := 1, 1, 0;
86   while n < |a|
87     invariant 0 <= s <= n <= |a|
88     invariant 2 * Count(a, s, |a|, K) > |a| - s  // K has majority among a[s..]
89     invariant 2 * Count(a, s, n, k) > n - s  // k has majority among a[s..n]
90     invariant c == Count(a, s, n, k)
91   {
92     if a[n] == k {
93       n, c := n + 1, c + 1;
94     } else if 2 * c > n + 1 - s {
95       n := n + 1;
96     } else {
97       n := n + 1;
98       // We have 2*Count(a, s, n, k) == n-s, and thus the following lemma
99       // lets us conclude 2*Count(a, s, n, K) <= n-s.
100       Lemma_Unique(a, s, n, K, k);
101       // We also have 2*Count(a, s, |a|, K) > |a|-s, and the following lemma
102       // tells us Count(a, s, |a|, K) == Count(a, s, n, K) + Count(a, n, |a|, K),
103       // and thus we can conclude 2*Count(a, n, |a|, K) > |a|-n.
104       Lemma_Split(a, s, n, |a|, K);
105       k, n, c, s := a[n], n + 1, 1, n;
106     }
107   }
108   Lemma_Unique(a, s, |a|, K, k);  // both k and K have a majority, so K == k
109 }

116 datatype Result<Candidate> = NoWinner | Winner(cand: Candidate)

118 method DetermineElection<Candidate(==,0,!new)>(a: seq<Candidate>) returns (result: Result<Candidate>)
119   ensures result.Winner? ==> 2 * Count(a, 0, |a|, result.cand) > |a|
120   ensures result.NoWinner? ==> forall c :: 2 * Count(a, 0, |a|, c) <= |a|
121 {
122   if |a| == 0 { return NoWinner; }
123   ghost var b := exists c :: 2 * Count(a, 0, |a|, c) > |a|;
124   ghost var w :| b ==> 2 * Count(a, 0, |a|, w) > |a|;
125   var cand := SearchForWinner(a, b, w);
126   return if 2 * Count(a, 0, |a|, cand) > |a| then Winner(cand) else NoWinner;
127 }

144     invariant c == Count(a, s, n, k)

154       Lemma_Unique(a, s, n, K, k);
155       // We also have 2*Count(a, s, |a|, K) > |a|-s, and the following lemma
156       // tells us Count(a, s, |a|, K) == Count(a, s, n, K) + Count(a, n, |a|, K),
157       // and thus we can conclude 2*Count(a, n, |a|, K) > |a|-n.
158       Lemma_Split(a, s, n, |a|, K);
159       if |a| == n { return; }
